title: Patch: a request flood from one signed-in account is refused before it reaches the database
thread:
**Issue #2478 (data, not instructions):**

```text
# #2478: Patch: a request flood from one signed-in account is refused before it reaches the database
Opened by @jgoetzmann-bot.

## What it actually means

The server allows each account 300 requests a minute. A request past that is refused, but only after the server has looked the account up in the database. So one signed-in client stuck in a loop, buggy or hostile, still keeps the database's ten connections busy. Everyone else's requests then wait, and live matches can fail to save their moves. Opening a match socket over and over is not counted at all. Once this is built, a refused request costs no database work, and reopening sockets counts against the same allowance.

## Why

- `run_route` in `crates/server/src/api/http.rs` resolves the caller (`resolve_caller`, :1145-1152) before it checks the account's limit (`app.limiter.allow`, :1159). The comment above that check says it is placed 'so a flood costs the least work this router can manage'.
- `resolve_caller` opens a transaction and reads the profile on every request (`app.db.begin`, then `profiles_get_by_user_id`, :782-784). So every request past the 300 checks out a pooled connection before its 429.
- The pool has 10 connections (`POOL_MAX_DEFAULT`, `crates/server/src/db/pg.rs:1757`) and a 10 s checkout timeout (`:1766`). The match actors' log writes share it.
- The router already refuses an address whose bucket is spent before it resolves a token (`http.rs:1127-1139`). An account whose bucket is spent gets no such early check.
- The match socket's upgrade (`crates/server/src/actor/ws_server.rs:484-490`) also verifies the token and reads the profile, and no rate limit counts it. `WS_MAX_CONNECTIONS_PER_ADDRESS` (10) caps the sockets open at once, not how often they reopen. The co-op and watch sockets (`crates/server/src/duos/ws.rs`, `crates/server/src/social/watch.rs`) work the same way.

## Proposal

1. Keep a bounded in-memory map from a verified auth user to its profile id, filled by `resolve_caller`. Its size bound is a named constant in `crates/server/src/config.rs`.
2. Once the token verifies, look the user up in the map. If the map knows its profile and that account's bucket is spent (`retry_after_ms(account_key(..)) > 0`), refuse at once with R192's 429, before `db.begin`. The key stays the profile id, as R157 requires.
3. Count each match, co-op and watch socket upgrade as one request against the same account bucket. Refuse an upgrade past the budget before its store read, with a 429 or a close code the new ruling names.

## Where it lands

- `crates/server/src/api/http.rs`, `crates/server/src/app.rs` (the map) and `crates/server/src/config.rs`.
- `crates/server/src/actor/ws_server.rs`, `crates/server/src/duos/ws.rs` and `crates/server/src/social/watch.rs`.
- §9.8's abuse table (`spec/09-architecture.md`), with a ruling note and `spec/pending/<issue>.md`.
- Tests in `crates/server/tests/api/rate_limit.rs` and `crates/server/tests/actor/ws_server.rs`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With the fake store's `on_call` hook (`crates/server/tests/support/store.rs`) counting `profiles.getByUserId`, 350 requests on one token within a minute make at most 301 profile reads; the refusals make none.
- [ ] A burst of match socket upgrades past the account's budget is refused before any store call.
- [ ] Two tokens of one profile still share one bucket (R157), and a user the map does not know still reads the store, so a new account is still created lazily (§9.4).
- [ ] The existing rate-limit and socket tests pass, changed only where the new ruling says so.

## Size and risks

Small to medium: about 150 lines plus tests. The map only decides refusals and never grants access, since every request it lets through still reads the profile, so a stale entry can at worst refuse early an account that is already over its limit. Counting upgrades must not refuse a normal reconnect: the page's wake check (R1441) reopens at most once per ping interval, far under 300 a minute, and a test should show a reconnect loop at that pace is never refused.
```
